title.en: 3.1 Pointer, Structure and Dynamic Memory Allocation

body.en:
A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable.

Declaration and use

int x = 10;
int *p;          /* declaration */
p = &x;          /* initialisation */
printf("%d", *p);   /* prints 10 */
int *q = NULL;   /* NULL pointer */
int **pp = &p;   /* pointer to pointer */

Pointer operators

  • & (address-of): gives the address of a variable. &x is the address of x.
  • * (indirection / value-at): gives the value stored at the address held by the pointer. *p is the value of x.

Important points

  • NULL pointer: a pointer that points to nothing (p = NULL). The last node of a linked list has next = NULL.
  • Pointer arithmetic: p + 1 moves by sizeof(data type) bytes. For an int pointer at address 1000, p + 1 is 1004 (4-byte int).
  • Pointer and array: the array name is the address of its first element, so a[i] = *(a + i).
  • Pointer to pointer: int **pp = &p; stores the address of another pointer; **pp is the value of x.
  • Size of every pointer is the same (4 bytes on 32-bit and 8 bytes on 64-bit systems), whatever type it points to.

Uses / advantages of pointers

  • Dynamic memory allocation (malloc, calloc).
  • Building dynamic data structures: linked list, tree, graph.
  • Call by reference: a function can change the caller's variables (swap).
  • Efficient handling of arrays and strings; returning more than one value.

A structure is a user-defined data type that groups related data items of different data types under one name. Each item is called a member (field).

Syntax and example

struct student {
    int roll;
    char name[20];
    float marks;
};
struct student s1 = {1, "Ravi", 78.5};
struct student s[60];  /* array */
s1.marks = 80;         /* dot operator */
  • The keyword struct defines the structure; the definition itself takes no memory.
  • Memory is allocated when a variable is declared (s1). Its size is at least the sum of the member sizes (the compiler may add padding).
  • Members are accessed using the dot (.) operator: s1.roll.
  • An array of structures stores many records, e.g. 60 students.

Array vs structure

ArrayStructure
Collection of elements of the same typeCollection of members of different types
Elements accessed by index a[i]Members accessed by name s.roll
Built-in (derived) typeUser-defined type (keyword struct)
e.g. marks of 60 studentse.g. one student's roll, name and marks

A pointer can store the address of a structure variable. Such a pointer is called a structure pointer.

struct student *ptr;
ptr = &s1;
ptr->roll = 5;       /* arrow operator */
(*ptr).roll = 5;     /* same meaning */
  • Members are accessed through a pointer with the arrow operator (->).
  • ptr->roll is the same as (*ptr).roll. The brackets are needed because . has higher precedence than *.
  • Passing a structure pointer to a function is faster than passing the whole structure (no copy is made).
  • Incrementing the pointer (ptr++) moves to the next structure in an array.

Self-referential structure

A structure that contains a pointer to a structure of the same type is called a self-referential structure. It is the building block of a linked list (and of trees).

struct node {
    int data;
    struct node *next;  /* same type */
};

Dynamic memory allocation means allocating memory at run time (during program execution) from the heap, as much as is actually needed. The functions are declared in <stdlib.h>.

Static vs dynamic allocation

Static allocationDynamic allocation
Memory allocated at compile timeMemory allocated at run time
Size is fixed and cannot changeSize can grow or shrink (realloc)
Memory may be wasted or be insufficientNo wastage: allocate as needed
Uses stack memoryUses heap memory
Freed automaticallyMust be freed with free()
e.g. int a[100];e.g. malloc(n * sizeof(int))

DMA functions

ptr = (type *) malloc(byte_size);
ptr = (type *) calloc(n, elem_size);
ptr = (type *) realloc(ptr, new_size);
free(ptr);
  1. malloc() (memory allocation): allocates one block of the given size in bytes. The memory contains garbage values. It returns a void * pointer, or NULL if memory is not available.
  2. calloc() (contiguous allocation): allocates n blocks of the given size and initialises all bytes to zero.
  3. realloc() (re-allocation): changes the size of previously allocated memory and keeps the old data.
  4. free(): releases dynamically allocated memory back to the heap.
int *a = (int *) malloc(5 * sizeof(int));
if (a == NULL)
    printf("Out of memory");
...
free(a);
a = NULL;   /* avoid dangling pointer */

malloc vs calloc

malloc()calloc()
One argument: total bytesTwo arguments: number of blocks and size of each
Memory has garbage valuesMemory is set to 0
Slightly fasterSlightly slower (initialisation)
  • Memory leak: allocated memory that is never freed.
  • Dangling pointer: a pointer that still holds the address of freed memory. Set it to NULL after free().

A linked list is a linear collection of data elements called nodes, in which the linear order is given by pointers. Each node points to the next node.

Node

Each node has two parts:

  • INFO (data) field: stores the actual data.
  • LINK (next) field: stores the address of the next node.
struct node {
    int data;
    struct node *next;  /* same type */
};

Representation

  • A pointer variable START (or HEAD) holds the address of the first node.
  • The LINK field of the last node contains NULL, which marks the end of the list.
  • If START = NULL, the list is empty.
  • Nodes are created with malloc() and need not be stored in continuous memory locations.

Creating a node

struct node *getnode(int x)
{
    struct node *nw;
    nw = (struct node *)
         malloc(sizeof(struct node));
    nw->data = x;
    nw->next = NULL;
    return nw;
}

Advantages

  • Dynamic size: grows and shrinks at run time; no memory wastage.
  • Easy insertion and deletion: only links change; no shifting of elements.
  • Used to implement stacks, queues, trees and graphs.

Disadvantages

  • Extra memory is needed for the pointer in every node.
  • No random access: to reach the n-th node all previous nodes must be visited (O(n)); binary search is not practical.
  • Reverse traversal is not possible in a singly linked list.

ArrayLinked list
Fixed size, decided at compile timeDynamic size, grows and shrinks at run time
Elements stored in continuous memoryNodes can be anywhere in memory
Random access by index: O(1)Sequential access only: O(n)
Insertion and deletion need shifting: O(n)Insertion and deletion change only links
No extra memory for linksExtra memory for a pointer in each node
Memory may be wasted (unused size)Memory is used as needed
Binary search possible (sorted)Only linear search
Static memory allocationDynamic memory allocation

1. Singly linked list

  • Each node has data and one pointer (next) to the next node.
  • The last node's next is NULL.
  • Traversal is possible in the forward direction only.

2. Circular linked list

  • A singly linked list in which the last node points back to the first node instead of NULL.
  • No node contains NULL. Any node can be the starting point, and the list can be traversed again and again.
  • Traversal stops when the pointer comes back to START (do … while (p != start)).
  • Used in round-robin CPU scheduling and multiplayer turn-taking games.

3. Doubly linked list

  • Each node has three parts: prev (address of the previous node), data and next (address of the next node).
  • The first node's prev and the last node's next are NULL.
  • Traversal is possible in both directions; deleting a given node is easier.
  • Needs more memory (two pointers per node).
  • Used in browser back/forward navigation and in undo/redo.
/* singly / circular */
struct node {
    int data;
    struct node *next;
};
/* doubly */
struct dnode {
    struct dnode *prev;
    int data;
    struct dnode *next;
};

A circular doubly linked list combines both: the last node's next points to the first node, and the first node's prev points to the last node.

Comparison

PointSinglyCircularDoubly
Pointers per node112
Last node's nextNULLfirst nodeNULL
Traversalforwardforward, circularforward and backward
Memorylesslessmore

1. Implementation of stack and queue without a size limit (dynamic stack and queue).
  2. Polynomial representation and arithmetic: each node stores a coefficient and an exponent, e.g. 5x³ + 4x² + 2 → (5,3) → (4,2) → (2,0).
  3. Dynamic memory management: the operating system keeps lists of free memory blocks.
  4. Representation of trees and graphs (adjacency list).
  5. Sparse matrix representation: only non-zero elements are stored.
  6. Undo/redo in editors and back/forward in browsers (doubly linked list).
  7. Music playlist and image viewer: next and previous item; a circular list repeats the playlist.
  8. Round-robin scheduling in an operating system (circular linked list).
  9. Large-number arithmetic: each node stores some digits of a very long number.

title.en: 3.3 Basic Operations on Singly Linked List

body.en:
The basic operations on a singly linked list are:

  • Traversal: visiting every node once.
  • Insertion: at the beginning, at the end, after or before a given node, in a sorted list.
  • Deletion: of the first node, the last node (or a given node).
  • Searching a node and counting the nodes.

Notation used in the algorithms

AlgorithmC codeMeaning
INFO(PTR)ptr->datadata of node PTR
LINK(PTR)ptr->nextaddress of the next node
getnode()malloc(…)create a new node
Free(PTR)free(ptr)release the node

Traversal algorithm

Algorithm TRAVERSE(START)
Step 1: Set PTR = START
Step 2: Repeat Steps 3 and 4
        while PTR != NULL
Step 3:   Process INFO(PTR)
Step 4:   Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 5: Exit

A temporary pointer PTR is used so that START is not lost. Traversal takes O(n) time.

h.en: 3.3.2 Insertion of a Node at the Beginning

body.en:
The new node becomes the first node, and START points to it.

Algorithm INSBEG(START, ITEM)
Step 1: [Create a new node]
        NEW = getnode()
        If NEW = NULL then
            Write "Overflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set INFO(NEW) = ITEM
Step 3: Set LINK(NEW) = START
Step 4: Set START = NEW
Step 5: Exit

C function

void ins_beg(int x)
{
    struct node *nw = getnode(x);
    nw->next = start;
    start = nw;
}
  • Order is important: first link the new node to the old first node (nw->next = start), and only then move START. If START is moved first, the rest of the list is lost.
  • The algorithm also works for an empty list: the new node's next becomes NULL.
  • Time complexity: O(1), because no traversal is needed.

h.en: 3.3.3 Insertion of a Node at the End

body.en:
The new node is attached after the current last node, and its link is NULL.

Algorithm INSEND(START, ITEM)
Step 1: NEW = getnode()
        If NEW = NULL then
            Write "Overflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set INFO(NEW) = ITEM
        Set LINK(NEW) = NULL
Step 3: If START = NULL then
            Set START = NEW and Exit
Step 4: Set PTR = START
Step 5: Repeat while LINK(PTR) != NULL
            Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 6: Set LINK(PTR) = NEW
Step 7: Exit

C function

void ins_end(int x)
{
    struct node *nw = getnode(x), *p;
    if (start == NULL) {
        start = nw;
        return;
    }
    p = start;
    while (p->next != NULL)
        p = p->next;
    p->next = nw;
}
  • The last node is the one whose LINK is NULL. The loop condition is p->next != NULL, not p != NULL, so that p stops on the last node.
  • If the list is empty, the new node becomes START.
  • Time complexity: O(n) because of the traversal. Keeping an extra LAST pointer makes it O(1).

h.en: 3.3.4 Insertion of a Node After / Before a Given Node

body.en:
(a) Insert after a given node (KEY)

Search for the node containing KEY, then place the new node between it and its next node.

Algorithm INSAFTER(START, KEY, ITEM)
Step 1: Set PTR = START
Step 2: Repeat while PTR != NULL and
        INFO(PTR) != KEY
            Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 3: If PTR = NULL then
            Write "Key not found" and Exit
Step 4: NEW = getnode()
        Set INFO(NEW) = ITEM
Step 5: Set LINK(NEW) = LINK(PTR)
Step 6: Set LINK(PTR) = NEW
Step 7: Exit

Important: Step 5 must be done before Step 6. If LINK(PTR) = NEW is done first, the address of the rest of the list is lost.

(b) Insert before a given node (KEY)

In a singly linked list we cannot move backwards, so a second pointer PREV follows one node behind PTR.

Algorithm INSBEFORE(START, KEY, ITEM)
Step 1: Set PTR = START, PREV = NULL
Step 2: Repeat while PTR != NULL and
        INFO(PTR) != KEY
            Set PREV = PTR
            Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 3: If PTR = NULL then
            Write "Key not found" and Exit
Step 4: NEW = getnode()
        Set INFO(NEW) = ITEM
        Set LINK(NEW) = PTR
Step 5: If PREV = NULL then
            Set START = NEW
        Else
            Set LINK(PREV) = NEW
Step 6: Exit
  • If KEY is in the first node, PREV stays NULL and the new node becomes the new START (same as insert at beginning).
  • Both operations take O(n) time in the worst case (searching for KEY).

h.en: 3.3.5 Insertion of a Node in a Sorted Linked List

body.en:
In a sorted (ascending) list, the new node must be inserted at its correct position so that the list stays sorted.

Algorithm INSORD(START, ITEM)
Step 1: NEW = getnode()
        Set INFO(NEW) = ITEM
Step 2: If START = NULL or
        ITEM < INFO(START) then
            Set LINK(NEW) = START
            Set START = NEW and Exit
Step 3: Set PTR = START
Step 4: Repeat while LINK(PTR) != NULL
        and INFO(LINK(PTR)) < ITEM
            Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 5: Set LINK(NEW) = LINK(PTR)
Step 6: Set LINK(PTR) = NEW
Step 7: Exit

Working

  • Case 1: the list is empty or ITEM is smaller than the first node → insert at the beginning.
  • Case 2: otherwise, move PTR while the next node's data is smaller than ITEM. PTR stops at the node after which ITEM must go (this also covers insertion at the end).
  • Example: inserting 25 into 10 → 20 → 30 → 40: PTR stops at 20 (because 30 > 25), so the list becomes 10 → 20 → 25 → 30 → 40.
  • Inserting every element this way builds a sorted list (the idea of insertion sort).

h.en: 3.3.6 Deleting the First and the Last Node

body.en:
(a) Delete the first node

Algorithm DELFIRST(START)
Step 1: If START = NULL then
            Write "Underflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set PTR = START
Step 3: Set START = LINK(START)
Step 4: Free(PTR)
Step 5: Exit
  • Save START in PTR, move START to the second node, then free the old first node. O(1).
  • Deleting from an empty list is underflow.

(b) Delete the last node

Algorithm DELLAST(START)
Step 1: If START = NULL then
            Write "Underflow" and Exit
Step 2: If LINK(START) = NULL then
            Free(START), Set START = NULL
            and Exit
Step 3: Set PREV = START
        Set PTR = LINK(START)
Step 4: Repeat while LINK(PTR) != NULL
            Set PREV = PTR
            Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 5: Set LINK(PREV) = NULL
Step 6: Free(PTR)
Step 7: Exit
  • Two pointers are needed: PTR reaches the last node and PREV the second-last. PREV becomes the new last node (its link is set to NULL).
  • Special case: if the list has only one node, START becomes NULL.
  • Time complexity: O(n).
  • Always free() the deleted node; otherwise memory leaks.

h.en: 3.3.7 Searching a Node and Counting the Nodes

body.en:
(a) Searching

Starting from START, each node's data is compared with ITEM until it is found or NULL is reached (linear search).

Algorithm SEARCH(START, ITEM)
Step 1: Set PTR = START, POS = 1
Step 2: Repeat while PTR != NULL
          If INFO(PTR) = ITEM then
              Write "Found at", POS
              and Exit
          Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
          Set POS = POS + 1
Step 3: Write "Not found"
Step 4: Exit
  • Best case O(1) (first node); worst case O(n) (last node or not present).
  • Binary search is not practical because there is no direct access to the middle node.

(b) Counting the nodes

Algorithm COUNT(START)
Step 1: Set COUNT = 0, PTR = START
Step 2: Repeat while PTR != NULL
          Set COUNT = COUNT + 1
          Set PTR = LINK(PTR)
Step 3: Return COUNT
  • Every node visited adds 1 to COUNT. An empty list gives 0.
  • Time complexity: O(n).

h.en: 3.3.8 Summary: Complete Program and Time Complexity

body.en:
The practical combines all operations in one menu-driven program (see the program below).

OperationTimePointer changes
Insert at beginningO(1)new→next = start; start = new
Insert at endO(n)last→next = new
Insert after nodeO(n)new→next = p→next; p→next = new
Insert in sorted listO(n)find position, then insert after
Delete firstO(1)start = start→next
Delete lastO(n)prev→next = NULL
Search / CountO(n)none (traversal only)

Common mistakes

  • Losing the list by moving START without saving it.
  • Not checking for an empty list (START = NULL) before deleting.
  • Not handling the one-node list when deleting the last node.
  • Forgetting to set the new last node's next to NULL.
  • Not freeing the deleted node.

title.en: Pointer basics: &, * and swapping using pointers

programs.out:
x = 10, *p = 10
after *p = 50, x = 50
p == &x ? yes
after swap: x = 20, y = 50

expl.en:
• p = &x stores the address of x in p; *p gives the value at that address.
  • Writing *p = 50 changes x itself, because p points to x.
  • swap() receives addresses (call by reference), so it can change the caller's variables.

title.en: Pointer arithmetic: traverse an array with a pointer

expl.en:
• The array name a is the address of the first element, so p = a.
  • *(p + i) is the same as a[i]. Adding 1 to an int pointer moves it by sizeof(int) bytes (4), not by 1 byte.

title.en: Structure: read and display student records

programs.out:
1 Ravi 78.5
2 Meena 91
3 Amit 66.5
Roll  Name      Marks
1     Ravi      78.5
2     Meena     91.0
3     Amit      66.5

expl.en:
• A structure groups related data of different types (int, char array, float) under one name.
  • An array of structures s[3] stores three complete records.
  • Members are accessed with the dot operator: s[i].roll.

title.en: Structure using pointer: find the topper with -> [Practical 5]

programs.out:
1 Ravi 78.5
2 Meena 91.0
3 Amit 66.0
4 Neha 88.0
Topper: Meena (91.0)

expl.en:
• ptr is a pointer to a structure; members are reached with the arrow operator ptr->marks, which is the same as (*ptr).marks.
  • ptr++ moves to the next record (by sizeof(struct student) bytes).
  • Passing a pointer to show() avoids copying the whole structure.

title.en: Dynamic memory: malloc for n numbers, then free

expl.en:
• The size n is known only at run time, so memory is taken from the heap with malloc().
  • malloc returns void * (cast to int *) or NULL if memory is not available, so always check it.
  • free(a) returns the memory. Forgetting it causes a memory leak.

title.en: calloc and realloc: grow an array at run time

expl.en:
• calloc(3, sizeof(int)) allocates 3 blocks and sets them all to 0 (malloc leaves garbage).
  • realloc resizes the block to 5 ints and keeps the old values 10, 20, 30.
  • The result is stored in a temporary pointer t first, so the old block is not lost if realloc fails.

title.en: Create a singly linked list of n nodes and display it

expl.en:
• Each node is a self-referential structure: data plus a pointer to the next node.
  • Every node is created with malloc. The first node becomes start; later nodes are joined with last->next = nw.
  • Keeping a last pointer makes each append O(1). Display walks from start until NULL.

title.en: Insert a node at the beginning and at the end

expl.en:
• Beginning: nw->next = start; start = nw;. No traversal, so O(1). The order matters: link first, then move start.
  • End: walk to the last node (the one whose next is NULL), then p->next = nw. This is O(n).
  • The empty-list case (start == NULL) must be handled separately.

title.en: Insert a node after / before a given node

expl.en:
• After key: find the key node p, then nw->next = p->next; p->next = nw;.
  • Before key: a second pointer prev trails one node behind p, because a singly list cannot move backwards. The new node goes between prev and p.
  • If the key is the first node (prev is NULL), the new node becomes the new start.

title.en: Insert into a sorted linked list (builds an ordered list)

expl.en:
• The list always stays in ascending order, whatever the input order.
  • If x is smaller than the first node (or the list is empty), it goes at the beginning.
  • Otherwise p stops at the last node whose next is not smaller than x, and the new node is inserted after p.
  • The output shows the list after every insertion: 5 goes at the front, 50 at the end, 20 in the middle.

title.en: Delete the first node and the last node

programs.out:
10 20 30 40 
deleted 10
20 30 40 
deleted 40
20 30 
deleted 30
deleted 20
List empty

expl.en:
• Delete first: save start in p, move start = start->next, then free(p). O(1).
  • Delete last: walk with p and prev until p is the last node, set prev->next = NULL, then free p. O(n).
  • Special cases: an empty list (underflow message) and a single node (start becomes NULL). The last call shows "List empty".

title.en: Search a node and count the nodes

programs.out:
Total nodes = 5
23 found at position 4
99 not found

expl.en:
• Both operations traverse the list from start to NULL.
  • count() adds 1 for every node visited.
  • search() compares each node's data with x and returns its position (1-based), or −1 if it reaches NULL.
  • A linked list has no index, so only linear search is possible (O(n)); binary search is not practical.

title.en: Singly linked list menu: insert, delete, search, count [Practical 6]

expl.en:
• The complete practical program: a menu-driven singly linked list.
  • Sample run: insert 20 and 30 at the end, 10 at the beginning → list 10 20 30; search 30 → position 3; delete first (10) and last (30) → only 20 remains.
  • display() also counts the nodes while printing them.
  • Each delete function handles the empty list; del_end also handles the single node case.

title.en: Circular linked list: create and display

expl.en:
• In a circular list the last node's next points back to the first node; no node contains NULL.
  • The traversal uses do … while (p != start): it stops when it comes round to start again. A p != NULL loop would never end.
  • last->next->data is 10, which proves the circle is closed.

title.en: Doubly linked list: display forward and backward

expl.en:
• Each node of a doubly linked list has two pointers: prev and next.
  • A new node's prev points to the old last node, and the old last node's next points to the new node.
  • So the list can be traversed in both directions: forward from start using next, backward from last using prev. The extra pointer costs more memory per node.

q.en: What is a pointer?

a.en: A variable that stores the memory address of another variable.

q.en: What do & and * do?

a.en: & gives the address of a variable; * gives the value stored at the address held by a pointer.

q.en: What is a NULL pointer?

a.en: A pointer that does not point to any valid memory (value NULL). The last node of a list has next = NULL.

q.en: If int *p holds 1000, what is p + 1?

a.en: 1004, because p + 1 moves by sizeof(int) = 4 bytes.

q.en: What is a structure?

a.en: A user-defined data type that groups members of different data types under one name.

q.en: Difference between . and -> ?

a.en: The dot operator accesses members through a structure variable; the arrow operator through a structure pointer.

q.en: What is a self-referential structure?

a.en: A structure that contains a pointer to a structure of the same type, e.g. a linked list node.

q.en: What is dynamic memory allocation?

a.en: Allocating memory at run time from the heap using malloc, calloc and realloc, and releasing it with free.

q.en: Difference between malloc and calloc?

a.en: malloc takes one argument and leaves garbage values; calloc takes two arguments and initialises memory to 0.

q.en: What does malloc return if memory is not available?

a.en: NULL.

q.en: What is a memory leak?

a.en: Memory allocated dynamically that is never freed.

q.en: What is a dangling pointer?

a.en: A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has been freed.

q.en: What is a linked list?

a.en: A linear collection of nodes in which each node contains data and the address of the next node.

q.en: What are the parts of a node?

a.en: INFO (data) field and LINK (next pointer) field.

q.en: What does START hold?

a.en: The address of the first node. START = NULL means the list is empty.

q.en: How is the end of a singly list identified?

a.en: The last node's next field is NULL.

q.en: Give two advantages of a linked list over an array.

a.en: Dynamic size; insertion and deletion without shifting elements.

q.en: Give two disadvantages of a linked list.

a.en: Extra memory for pointers; no random access, so access is O(n).

q.en: What are the types of linked list?

a.en: Singly, circular and doubly linked lists (and circular doubly).

q.en: What is a circular linked list?

a.en: A list in which the last node points back to the first node instead of NULL.

q.en: What is a doubly linked list?

a.en: A list whose nodes have prev and next pointers, so it can be traversed in both directions.

q.en: Give applications of linked list.

a.en: Dynamic stack and queue, polynomial representation, graphs (adjacency list), undo/redo, playlists.

q.en: What is the time complexity of inserting at the beginning?
Why is insertion at the end O(n)?

a.en: We must traverse the whole list to reach the last node (unless a LAST pointer is kept).

q.en: Why is a PREV pointer needed to insert before a node?

a.en: A singly list cannot move backwards, so PREV keeps the address of the node before PTR.

q.en: What is underflow in a linked list?

a.en: Trying to delete from an empty list (START = NULL).

q.en: Which search can be applied on a linked list?

a.en: Only linear search, because there is no direct access to the middle node.

q.en: What happens if START is moved before linking the new node?

a.en: The address of the rest of the list is lost.
